title: PR #6490 moved structure-board rendering into a new generic render_object_structure admin endpoint and dropped the user_can_change_page check the old details() path applied, so any staff user can read the plugin structure of pages they may not view.

findings.explanation: The flagged line (cms/tests/test_alias.py:214) is `context = self.get_context(path=get_object_edit_url(target_page_content))`. This is a test file that builds a URL string to pass to a test client's get_context helper; it does not construct or execute any SQL. The `get_object_edit_url` function (cms/toolbar/utils.py:122-129) merely resolves an admin URL via `admin_reverse('cms_placeholder_render_object_edit', args=[content_type.pk, obj.pk])` using integer primary keys — no SQL string is built or executed. The Semgrep rule is a heuristic that matched the word 'sql-sink' pattern, but there is no SQL injection sink here: no query string concatenation, no raw SQL, and no user-controlled input reaching any database call. This is a false positive.

findings.explanation: The new render_object_structure view fetches an arbitrary object by user-controlled content_type_id and object_id (cms/views.py:191-205) and renders it with no ownership/permission check. The base code that this PR replaces gated the same structure rendering behind user_can_change_page(request.user, page) (cms/views.py:168-170 base). The PR removes that check and exposes the endpoint via the admin URL (cms/admin/placeholderadmin.py:212), so any authenticated staff user can request the structure of any object id, leaking objects they are not permitted to edit. The policy states that when CMS_PERMISSION is on, editors need explicit permission over specific pages/objects, and 'Can use Structure mode' is a distinct permission — none of which is verified here.

evidence.content:
pat(r'^object/([0-9]+)/edit/([0-9]+)/$', render_object_edit),
            pat(r'^object/([0-9]+)/structure/([0-9]+)/$', render_object_structure),
            pat(r'^object/([0-9]+)/preview/([0-9]+)/$', render_object_preview),

Most of these offer the usual add/change/delete options, though there are some exceptions, such as ``cms | placeholder | Can use Structure mode``. ... When ``CMS_PERMISSION`` is enabled, unless you simply make your users superusers, you'll need to give each one either global permission, or permission over specific pages

findings.suggested_fix: Before rendering, verify the requesting user has permission to access/edit the specific object (e.g., resolve the owning page and call user_can_change_page(request.user, page), or check the object's own has_change_permission), and return 403/404 otherwise.

findings.explanation: render_object_edit (cms/views.py:208-226) fetches an arbitrary object by user-controlled content_type_id/object_id and then dispatches to that object's resolved view (match.func) with no ownership/permission check. It only verifies the model is editable and that the object has get_absolute_url. Any authenticated staff user can supply an object id they do not own and trigger its edit view, exposing/acting on objects they are not authorized for. The policy requires per-object permission checks when CMS_PERMISSION is on.

evidence.content: pat(r'^object/([0-9]+)/edit/([0-9]+)/$', render_object_edit),
When ``CMS_PERMISSION`` is enabled, unless you simply make your users superusers, you'll need to give each one either global permission, or permission over specific pages

findings.suggested_fix: Add an authorization check confirming the requesting user may edit the specific object (e.g., user_can_change_page on the owning page or the object's has_change_permission) before resolving and dispatching to its view.
